## The curator's role and decisions

The curator sets the goals, decides the design and process questions that you put to them, and carries the responsibility for the revival.

The revival resolves the contradictions that the team left, by the evidence in the repository: the specification, the papers, the library and the code. The curator does not redesign the language, and decides a contradiction that the evidence leaves open, by the designers' intent. The curator's words show what the curator decided. They are not the ground of the design.

Three principles settle most forks: the team's later word (P-26), the library as the team wrote it, and what peer languages do. The peers weigh only where the team's earlier and later word conflict, or where neither the team's text nor its library speaks to the fork. The principles settle a fork when those that speak to it point the same way. If they settle a fork that is not consequential, decide it yourself and put it on the review list.

Weigh a team text by its provenance: who wrote it, in which role, such as a core designer or an outside contributor of the open-source years, and whether the team reviewed it or its author called it provisional. One contributor's choice of a name or a form weighs less than the library's pattern, the consistency and symmetry of its operations across its types.

A decision is consequential if it:

- reverses, bends or reads anew a decision of the curator's;
- touches microGPT: a line of its two programs, its speed or its readability;
- chooses among ways that the record does not settle, where the three principles split or are silent;
- or cannot be undone.

It reaches the curator in one of three ways:

1. **Asked before the work.** A known fork is probed, and put as an ask before the batch is briefed.
2. **Landed, then reviewed.** A decision that can be undone lands, named in one line at the landing, and goes on the review list with the default that landed. Put it to the curator later, one per message.
3. **A hold.** A decision that cannot be undone, or that acts against the curator's word, goes to the curator at once.

Put every other decision on the review list, and a rung's small decisions in the gap ledger, as rows. Neither holds up the work.

- Launch a probe or an Opus worker without asking. Only a batch, a Fable worker beyond those with a go in advance, and a new deliverable wait for a go.
- Launch a batch only on the curator's explicit go. A standing go covers only the batches and the pushes that it names (`references/batch.md`).
- Before you ask the curator anything, or measure anything, search the record (below). If it settles the question, act on it. An entry's history is part of that search, and is read before any claim about the entry's reasons, since the history keeps the ground and the curator's words that the entry's text leaves out.
- If a decision that a worker wrote in one line of its report is consequential, it is not made until the curator sees it. Bring it by one of the three ways.
- A worker that looks for issues gives all its findings the same weight. Sort the findings yourself, by what each needs, before any finding reaches the curator or goes into the next brief:
  - If a finding would change a decision of the curator's, put it to the curator as an ask. No other finding becomes an ask.
  - If a reason in the record is no longer true, cut it. You need no approval to bring the record in line with reality.
  - If a finding corrects the ground of an entry and changes no decision, put it in the entry's history. It changes nothing that a reader does.
  - If a finding confirms a decision, give it one line.
- Keep a proposal of yours marked as yours until the curator says yes.
- Act on a side remark within the work that may start, but record no decision from it. Write a one-time go nowhere: the launch or the commit is its trace.
- When something goes wrong or is undecided, find the cause and choose the best way forward for the whole. If that choice is consequential, bring it by one of the three ways. Do not roll back or bisect.
- Weigh a rule by what it protects against what it costs. If its words would defeat its purpose, do the better thing, say so in one line, and propose a fix. Propose one too when a file grows or a rule makes clutter.
- Have the skill writer add, change or remove a rule of this skill, in `SKILL.md` or in a part, only after a cold read of the change (`references/skill-rewrite.md`, "The method"). A fix of a path or a section name is a change too, except at an approved draft's landing (`references/skill-rewrite.md`, "The method", step 7). The writer's fixes of the cold read's flags land with no second cold read. Then the change lands without the curator's yes, also when you proposed it, unless the bullet after next says that it waits. A line of `references/sources.md` is not a rule, and needs neither a cold read nor a report.
- After a change to this skill or to `fortress-repo` lands, have a worker update that skill's page: the page of skill drafts or the page of `fortress-repo` changes, whose links the boot note holds (`references/skill-rewrite.md`, "The method", step 7). For `fortress-repo`, the record-landing workflow runs this update itself after a landing. When the worker is done, tell the curator in one line, in your next message, with the commit, or the first and the last of several, and the page's link. Watch both pages for comments sent to Claude. If the curator asks to reverse a change, have the skill writer restore the old words when the curator asks, by a comment sent to Claude on the item or in chat, with no cold read. The reversal does not wait for the end of the curator's reading. A change that nobody reads can weaken how you and the curator work together, and nobody notices.

302	- **Walk** is the interpreter. The **compiled path** first checks a program's types with the **checker**, then writes JVM bytecode with the **code generator**.
303	- The **prelude** is the small library that the compiled path uses today. The **one library** is the interpreter's library. The **switch-over** is the move of the compiled path onto the one library, after which the prelude is deleted.

Each problem that only the one library shows is then fixed as its own small change, with its own test, under the full check.

306	- A **rung** is one change. One worker builds it, and a second, the skeptic, checks it. A **run** is one launch of the batch workflow. The **gate** is the full check before a run lands.

309	- The **ledger** is the list of known defects. A **row** is one defect. An **expected-failure test** is a test that is known to fail and is marked so.

# The check of climb batch 33's record before its launch

## For the curator

**What I checked.** I read the record as a new reader. I ran each of run 1's failing programs once, on a scratch tree with the code of `main`. I read each decision that a rung names, with its history. I read the carriers' review, ways C and D and its three forms. I checked whether the rungs of each run can be merged, and whether the cost fits the last batch.

**What I found.**

- **No fork needs your answer before the launch.** The form of the prelude's number types is your decision P-178. Its detail is the review's way D, which uses way C's code generator. Inside way C the review recommends form 2. Review-queue item 513 says that the choice between forms 1 and 2 is the planner's, not yours.
- **Every program of run 1 fails today as the record says,** with the message that it gives. One description was too wide (rung V, below).

That does not bend what you said: your words were to take microGPT's slice first if probe Y works. But the entry's words need a change after the landing. I put that on your review list in the record.

## A. Changes of the record that I made

Each has one reason. Section 1 of the record is the manifest's source. I did not edit it. Where a change of a rung's section needs the same change there, I say so.

1. **Rung V, row 822's form (section 2, and section 4, V, step 1).** The record said that a `typecase` inside a generic function "whose arms name its type parameters" stops. Reason: my first reproducer of that description compiles and runs.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# spend.py <since-epoch> <file-or-dir>...: tokens written (input + cache creation) and read, per transcript, deduplicated by message id
# the coordinating session's own transcript (fe616d40) is left out; agents: <session-dir>/subagents/*.jsonl or a task output file; claude -p runs: the project directory
import json, os, sys, glob
since=float(sys.argv[1]); files=[]
for a in sys.argv[2:]:
    files += [a] if os.path.isfile(a) else glob.glob(os.path.join(a,'*.jsonl'))
tw=tr=0; n=0
for f in sorted(set(files)):
    if os.path.getmtime(f) < since or os.path.basename(f).startswith("fe616d40"): continue
    seen={}; 
    for line in open(f, errors='replace'):
        try: r=json.loads(line)
        except Exception: continue
        m=r.get('message') if isinstance(r.get('message'),dict) else None
        if not m or 'usage' not in m: continue
        seen[m.get('id') or id(m)]=m['usage']
    w=sum(u.get('input_tokens',0)+u.get('cache_creation_input_tokens',0) for u in seen.values())
    rd=sum(u.get('cache_read_input_tokens',0) for u in seen.values())
    if seen: n+=1; tw+=w; tr+=rd; print(f"{os.path.basename(f)[:40]:40} calls={len(seen):4} written={w/1e3:8.1f}K read={rd/1e6:6.2f}M")
print(f"TOTAL files={n} written={tw/1e6:.2f}M read={tr/1e6:.2f}M")
======

#

#     word (rung, resume, repair, skeptic, skeptic2, judge, gather, review, gate, coldread, commit), a retry
#     counted with its role, a repair or judge on the merged tree (label repair:review, judge:gate ...) apart;
#   first calls: the writes of each agent's first message, and how many started cold (over 30K written by the

#     those that run the library order (a fortress compile of CompilerLibrary);

#   refusal cycles: per rung, the agents after its first skeptic (judge, repair, resume, skeptic2) and what
#     they wrote.
import glob, json, os, re, sys
from datetime import datetime

def ts(s):
    try:
        return datetime.fromisoformat(s.replace('Z', '+00:00')).timestamp()
    except Exception:
        return None

def role_of(label):
    base = re.sub(r':attempt\d+$', '', label)
    parts = base.split(':')
    head = parts[0]
    if head in ('repair', 'judge') and len(parts) > 1 and parts[1] in ('review', 'gate'):
        return head + ':merged'
    if head in ('gate2',) or base.startswith('gate:'):
        return 'gate'
    return head

def rung_of(label):
    base = re.sub(r':attempt\d+$', '', label)

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# tx.py FILE...: per transcript: label, first and last record time, writes (input+cache creation, dedup by message id), messages, first message's writes, models
import json, sys, os, datetime
def ts(s):
    return datetime.datetime.fromisoformat(s.replace('Z','+00:00')).timestamp()
def label(f):
    m=f[:-6]+'.meta.json'
    try:
        d=json.load(open(m)); return d.get('description','?')
    except Exception: return '?'
def study(f):
    seen={}; order=[]; first=last=None; models={}
    for line in open(f, errors='replace'):
        try: r=json.loads(line)
        except Exception: continue
        t=r.get('timestamp')
        if t:
            tt=ts(t); first=tt if first is None else min(first,tt); last=tt if last is None else max(last,tt)
        m=r.get('message') if isinstance(r.get('message'),dict) else None
        if not m or 'usage' not in m: continue
        k=m.get('id') or id(m)
        if k not in seen: order.append(k)
        seen[k]=m['usage']
        if m.get('model'): models[m['model']]=models.get(m['model'],0)+1
    w=lambda u:u.get('input_tokens',0)+u.get('cache_creation_input_tokens',0)
    tot=sum(w(u) for u in seen.values())
    fw=w(seen[order[0]]) if order else 0
    return dict(label=label(f), first=first, last=last, writes=tot, msgs=len(seen), firstw=fw, models=models, mtime=os.path.getmtime(f))
if __name__=='__main__':
    rows=[]
    for f in sys.argv[1:]:
        d=study(f); d['f']=os.path.basename(f); rows.append(d)
    rows.sort(key=lambda d:d['first'] or 0)
    T=0
    for d in rows:
        fm=lambda x: datetime.datetime.utcfromtimestamp(x).strftime('%m-%d %H:%M:%S') if x else '-'
        dur=(d['last']-d['first'])/60 if d['first'] else 0
        T+=d['writes']
        print(f"{d['f'][:24]:24} {d['label'][:30]:30} {fm(d['first'])} {fm(d['last'])} {dur:6.1f}m w={d['writes']/1e3:7.1f}K msgs={d['msgs']:4} first={d['firstw']/1e3:6.1f}K {','.join(f'{k}:{v}' for k,v in d['models'].items())}")
    print(f"TOTAL {len(rows)} {T/1e6:.3f}M")
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# brief.py RUN_DIR: per agent, the calls that print its briefing (facts-extract.sh with 4 or more record keys, its --part continuations),
# the first one's call index, assistant-message index and seconds after start, the parts read, and the results' chars and estimated tokens (0.40 a char + 110 a call)
import json, os, re, sys, glob
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(__file__))
from calls_mod import calls
KEY=re.compile(r'"(?:P-\d+|F-\d+|ledger:\d+|doc:[^"]+|code:[^"]+|map:[^"]+)"')
tot=0
for f in sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(sys.argv[1],'agent-*.jsonl'))):
    lab=json.load(open(f[:-6]+'.meta.json')).get('description','')
    cs=calls(f)
    # first message: does the brief hold a briefing command?
    first=open(f).read(400000)
    hasb = 'Your briefing' in first or 'briefing' in first
    bc=[]
    for d in cs:
        inp=d['input'] if isinstance(d['input'],dict) else {}
        cmd=inp.get('command','') or ''
        if 'facts-extract' in cmd and len(KEY.findall(cmd))>=4:
            bc.append(d)
    if not bc:
        print(f"{lab:12} {os.path.basename(f)[6:14]} briefing calls: none   (brief mentions briefing: {hasb})"); continue
    chars=sum(d['rchars'] for d in bc); tok=0.40*chars+110*len(bc); tot+=tok
    parts=[re.search(r'--part (\d+)', (d['input'].get('command') or '')) for d in bc]
    parts=[p.group(1) if p else '1' for p in parts]
    d0=bc[0]
    saved=sum(1 for d in bc if 'Output too large' in d['rtext'] or 'saved to' in d['rtext'][:300])
    print(f"{lab:12} {os.path.basename(f)[6:14]} first at call {d0['i']} msg {d0['msg']} {round(d0['t'])}s; calls {len(bc)} parts {','.join(parts)}; {chars} chars ~{tok/1e3:.1f}K tok; saved-to-file {saved}")
print('total ~%.0fK'%(tot/1e3))

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The standard and the sources

POSITIONS.md:30
- P-33 **The work toward microGPT compiled follows the phases, in the order that the curator approved, and the rest of the switch-over takes microGPT's slice first.** These phases are steps of the work, not the compiler's phases, and they are numbered 3 to 6, after two earlier ones. Phase 3 ends when the compiled checker reports no error on the apis and components of the interpreter's library that the distance to the switch-over counts (F-53 defines the distance, says what it counts and holds its value). The library's other components are not part of phase 3: each is cleared before the first program that needs it, and at the latest before walk runs the checker (P-12), so `System` by the switch-over, since the compiler's tests need it (F-293); F-290 counts their errors. Phase 4, the switch-over: first the natives, the library's `builtinPrimitive` bindings made to run on the compiled path, then the compiled path reads the interpreter's library and the compiler's prelude is deleted; phase 5, microGPT compiles: its static types, the array design and the code generator's open gaps; phase 6, microGPT runs fast. The rest of phase 4 takes microGPT's slice first: the compile command selects the one library beside the prelude, one build serving both by a second set of the run time's value classes (F-353), so that each wall that only a tree switched onto the one library shows is met as one rung with its own test on `main`, under the gate, beside the code generator's walls; the move of the compiled tests and the prelude's deletion come last. Why: those walls stand one behind another (F-352), and this way gates each one, where the whole switch-over first lands them in one piece that no gate checks in parts. Code-generator work goes on beside that order, under either library (P-37). Row 320, an api implemented by a component of another name does not link, is part of the switch-over's design.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The one library and the compiled checker

POSITIONS.md:35
- P-37 **One library, the interpreter's, is the library that the compiler checks.** The interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`, becomes the compiled path's prelude in place of the compiler's own, and the compiled path reads the interpreter's library with it. Why: the switch-over spares porting the interpreter's library into the compiler's; the revival develops the checker until it accepts that fuller library. The curator sees the compiler's prelude, its own library files `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin` and `CompilerAlgebra`, as a bootstrap to remove. So no declaration is added to the compiler's prelude, and at the switch-over its three files are deleted and their tests kept (P-38 says which tests are respelled; F-293 holds the compiler's fourth file, `CompilerSystem`). There are two exceptions, each so that both paths do the same before the switch-over, and each copy goes with the prelude: the numerals, where the prelude carries the design of P-174 and P-176; and the built-in number types, where it takes the form of P-178. The decision settles which files survive, not the designs inside them: the one library takes a design of the prelude's where it is the team's later decision, as it took the prelude's flat shape of the number types. This decision does not stop work on the code generator, which is compiler work under either library.

POSITIONS.md:75
- P-167 **The three natives over `Any`: `ilkName` and `SEQV` name the compiled path's helpers, which walk's loader answers with its own operations, and `Object`'s `asString` is written in Fortress as `self.ilkName`.** `ilkName` and `SEQV` keep P-58's form, a bare `builtinPrimitive("…")`, naming `stringOps.typeName` and `equality.sEquiv`. The compiled path runs each helper as it does today, and the helper's answer is the operation's definition. Walk's loader (`interpreter/glue/NativeApp.java`, where it reads a `builtinPrimitive` string) holds a table of eight names, these two among them (F-335), and answers each with walk's own operation, as a virtual machine runs its own code for an intrinsic; no implementation is shared, and one test runs on both paths to hold the two together. For these two names P-58's walk half, that walk loads the named helper, bends. P-169 makes the device the rule for the runtime's own operations, 45 more bindings. `Object`'s `asString` becomes `self.ilkName`, P-91's rule as text, which removes one native and, once the compiled path reads the one library, the compiled stack overflow of row 321. The ilk is the trait's name on both paths, such as `ZZ32` and never walk's `Int`, so walk's native objects stop being types that a program sees or prints; its five native number objects go altogether (P-178). What `SEQV` answers is P-168. Why: the compiled path's answer is the definition and walk is brought in line, the curator's "do it the way the compiler path does it"; the three are the runtime's own operations, not calls into Java helpers. Detail: `reviews/any-carrier-2026-11-06.md`, section 6, options (c) and (e1).

POSITIONS.md:58
- P-60 **The specification reads a `comprises` clause at the level of values.** `trait S comprises { U, V }` says that every value of `S` is a value of `U` or of `V`. So another trait may stand between `S` and its listed types. The specification defines "covers" once: a type covers another when every value of the second is a value of the first. The Meet Rule gains a case for closed traits. Where the rule asks for a declaration at the meet of two overloads' parameter types, several declarations below both serve, if together they cover the meet. So a call whose argument's static type stands between closed traits and their listed types may have several most specific declarations. The call's type is the intersection of their return types, and the declaration that runs is unique only at run time. The compiled checker uses coverage only in its overloading rules, to accept an overload set and to justify a call's tie among several most specific declarations, and not in its general subtype test. Why: the proof addendum (`reviews/comprises-type-level-proof-addendum.md`) shows this sound for ground declarations, at calls that need no coercion. A ground declaration's types hold no type variable, and `G[\ZZ32\]` is ground. The addendum shows it for coverage used only in that way, and leaves any wider use to a review of its own. A call that needs a coercion is outside the proof too (F-76 gives what the compiled checker does there). A declaration with static parameters, whose instance dispatch must choose at run time, is outside the proof: one instance would have to meet every one of the return types at once. The typing by the intersection is not extended to it, and the specification states that boundary. Rows 543 and 551: the compiled checker gives no call an intersection type where any declaration of the family has static parameters, and walk checks no `comprises` clause declared outside the main component.

POSITIONS.md:60
- P-146 **In a self-typed trait, the compiled checker types `self` in the method bodies as also being the implementing type.** A self-typed trait is a trait `C[\X\]` whose parameter `X` extends `C[\X\]`, such as `Integral[\I extends Integral[\I\]\]`. In its method bodies, `self` has the type `C[\X\] & X`. The method signatures keep the plain trait type. Only the overloading check's exclusion test reads `self` in a signature as `C[\X\] & X` (P-157). The checker refuses a type that extends such a trait at another type, since an extender must be a subtype of the static argument that it gives: `object Bad extends Integral[\ZZ32\]` is refused, because `Bad` is not a `ZZ32`. Scala has the same rule for self types. The library's text gains no self type and no `comprises` clause, and walk is unchanged. The rule accepts every self-typed method body of the library except `Integral`'s `numerator`, which each integer type declares instead. Why: the checker reads the library as the team wrote it, as P-44 does for the closure of `AnyIntegral`, by one rule that peer languages share. F-225 states the rule as built.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### Numbers

POSITIONS.md:104
- P-173 **A numeral converts where it stands: where its place fixes a type, into that type at compile time from its exact value; where nothing fixes one, into the machine default, a `ZZ32`, or a `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit, and with a radix point an `RR64`.** A place fixes a type when its declared type has a coercion from the numeral type, as the eight number types have and a program's own type may (P-174); `Any`, `Object`, `Number`, an unbounded type parameter and no declared type take the default. So `x = 3` is a `ZZ32`, and `x SEQV z` is `true` for `z: ZZ32 = 3`; `bigN = 3000000000` is a `ZZ64` at its binding (row 946). The default applies to a numeral, a literal after the fold, never to an expression of a numeral type, and a `nat` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32` where it is a size (P-40), and a `ZZ` where it is one of a numeral type's four numbers (P-174). A type parameter that several numerals fix takes the narrowest default that holds every value, an `RR64` where any has a radix point, each numeral converting into it exactly; a float numeral whose conversions into `QQ` and `RR64` tie reads `RR64`. At a typed place the conversion is exact or rounds once (P-76, P-172), and a numeral outside the type's range is refused statically; walk converts from the exact value at the same places, place by place, before it runs the checker (P-12). An expression of numerals alone folds exactly before the checker into a signed constant, which defaults as an integer numeral, as a `QQ` for a quotient, or as an `RR64` with a radix point: so `x = 7/2` is a `QQ`, `1/2 = 0.5` is `true`, and `-2147483648`, prefix minus on a numeral, folded, is a `ZZ32`. `gg(5, w)`, with `gg` declared at `(ZZ32, T)` and at `(Any, Any)`, runs the `ZZ32` declaration (P-49). The parameter types of the declaration that a call runs are places that fix a type, and a numeral argument goes to the most specific declaration that takes it, by its own conversion if need be, with its default as the last resort: `u = 0` is `true` for `u: NN32 = 0`, the numeral an `NN32` at `NN32`'s own `=` (P-46 gives the rule and its ground; row 1016 holds where walk departs, and row 1017 where both paths do). Why: the design completes the Working Draft's, whose numerals have types of their own so that a library decides by coercions how they meet other types (P-174 gives that ground). It bends P-26 in two places, the numeral types, whose names and static parameters are the Draft's (P-174), and the places that fix no type, where the compiler's prelude, the team's later word, keeps the numeral's own type; the curator takes the bend by his right to finish the specification. He declined exact defaults, `ZZ` and `QQ` (the 2012 restart gives `NN` and `QQ`, `literals.tick:25`), since microGPT's untyped hyperparameters (`MicroGptFlat.fss:18`) would then be rationals and every untyped index would need `asZZ32`. The Draft's text that it contradicts, for Appendix I: numerals "not directly converted" and "polymorphic" (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:132-141`) at places that fix no type, and a `nat` parameter usable wherever an `NN32` variable is (`basic/trait-parameters.tex:84-86`); P-174 names the binary chapter's, which it leaves out. What it keeps and changes in form: the judgement's section 3, but for the numeral types' form, which P-174 holds. Detail: `reviews/literal-design-judgement-2026-11-08.md`, sections 1 to 6 and the 42 test programs of its appendix; the prototype, `compile-ladder/plan-29/probes/literal-default.md`.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The one library and the compiled checker

POSITIONS.md:62
- P-148 **The checker's speed comes right after its correctness in priority: a rung that changes the compiled checker also makes the change fast.** The rung times the checker before and after its change. It first makes the change correct. Then, in the same rung, it makes the new code fast, without changing which programs the checker accepts or refuses. So no optimization is left to be done by hand after the landing. Why: the checker must stay usable as it grows. Some slowdown is fine, but new checks have made it orders of magnitude slower, so that the checker ran past the time limit of the batch gate's count stage, and rungs could not land. The timing is a smoke test: one run of each tree, to catch a slowdown of several times; a small difference is noise. The `fortress-repo` skill (`compiler.md`, "The checker's time") gives the steps, their commands and what the rung reports.

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%

\section{Typecase Expressions}
\seclabel{typecase}

\note{This section should be revised according to the changes in the pattern matching proposal.}

\note{Do we want to support \EXP{\KWD{typecase} \mathord{\KWD{self}} \KWD{of} \ldots}?

How about \EXP{\KWD{typecase} (x, \KWD{self}, y) \KWD{of} \ldots}?

...

\emph{TypecaseVars} &::=& \emph{BindId} \\
&$|$& \texttt{(} \emph{BindId}(\EXP{,} \emph{BindId})$^+$ \texttt{)} \\

\emph{TypecaseClauses} &::=& \emph{TypecaseClause}$^+$\\

\emph{TypecaseClause} &::=&
\emph{TypecaseTypes} \EXP{\Rightarrow} \emph{BlockElems} \\

\emph{TypecaseTypes}
&::=& \texttt{(} \emph{TypeList} \texttt{)}\\
&$|$& \emph{Type} \\

\emph{CaseElse} &::=& \KWD{else} \EXP{\Rightarrow} \emph{BlockElems}\\

\end{Grammar}

A \KWD{typecase} expression begins with \KWD{typecase} followed by
an identifier or a sequence of parenthesized identifiers,
optionally followed by the token \EXP{=} and a \emph{binding} expression,
followed by \KWD{of}, a sequence of typecase clauses
(each consisting of a sequence of \emph{guarding types}
followed by the token \EXP{\Rightarrow}, followed by an expression block),
an optional \KWD{else} clause
(consisting of \KWD{else} followed by the token \EXP{\Rightarrow},
followed by an expression block),
and finally \KWD{end}.

A \KWD{typecase} expression with a binding expression
evaluates the expression first;
if it completes normally, the value of the expression is bound
to the identifiers and the first matching typecase clause is chosen.
If there are multiple identifiers, the binding expression must be evaluated
to a tuple value of the same number of elements.
A typecase clause matches if the type of the value bound to each identifier
is a subtype of the corresponding type in the clause.
The expression block of the first matched clause
(and only that clause) is evaluated (see \secref{block-expr}) to yield
the value of the \KWD{typecase} expression.
If no matched clause is found, a \TYP{MatchFailure} exception is thrown
(\TYP{MatchFailure} is an unchecked exception).
Unlike bindings in other contexts,
the static type of such an identifier
is \emph{not} determined by the static type of
the expression it is bound to.
If the static type of a subexpression
in the bindings for a \KWD{typecase} expression has type \VAR{T},
when typechecking each typecase clause,
the static type of the corresponding identifier is the intersection of \VAR{T}
and the corresponding guarding type for that clause.
The type of a \KWD{typecase} expression is the union
of types of all right-hand sides of the typecase clauses.

FACTS.md:170
- F-352 **A compiled program has run against the interpreter's library only in a scratch tree with twelve marked hacks; on `main` the compile command selects the compiler's prelude unless `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one` selects the one library (F-381).** In that tree, on `832f7d0d91`'s code, two lines of `Shell.useCompilerLibraries()` point the compiled path at the one library, and a one-line program then passes the checker and the code generator. Its run needs the library's fourteen components as bytecode, compiled by name in about 200 s. Three programs ran and printed walk's output: one that prints a line, one that builds and reads an `Array1`, and a dot product in the program's own loop over two `Array1`. Not run: an array of rank 2 or 3 (row 992, fixed since), the library's `DOT` and `SUM` (row 732, fixed since), and microGPT, which the checker stops (F-58). The runs met sixteen walls of two kinds. A test compiled against the prelude can show the first kind: the refusal of varargs (row 624), `label` (row 81), a closure class written twice (row 315), a method written twice (row 990), a missing cast at a `comprises` type (row 991), and rows 992 and 732; rows 81, 990, 991, 732 and 992 are fixed since, and rows 624 and 315 stand. Only a tree switched onto the one library shows the second kind: which run-time class carries each built-in type, a choice that reaches the code generator's naming (rows 874, 995 and 866); the trait table's search by the prelude's api names (row 942); the dispatch method's package (row 994); `NN32`'s two getters (row 993). Every run had the JVM's verifier off, so the number of emitted methods that the verifier refuses is not known. A program's check takes about a second under either library on warm caches, and 17 s against the one library on cold caches, one run each. Measured once; nothing landed, and no test holds it. The walls grouped, against PLAN's phase 4 and phase 5 lines"; `compile-ladder/plan-31/probes/model-closure-check.md`, "4. The checker's time for one program".

## The compiler's prelude, until the switch-over

The compiled path uses the compiler's own prelude: `LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss`, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss` and `Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss`. `Library/CompilerSystem.fss` is the compiled path's `System`.

Do not add a declaration to the three prelude files: the switch-over deletes them, and their tests stay. Two exceptions (P-37): its numeral types and coercions follow `revival-changes.md`, "Numbers", and a brief may ask to declare each built-in number type as one `value object`, the form that both libraries are to take. If a helper of `nativeHelpers/` that the one library binds is wrong, fix the helper's Java, even if the prelude binds it, and leave the prelude's text: its binding gives the fix. Change with it a compiled test that pinned the old result.

## The `fortress` commands

`Shell.java` dispatches `bin/fortress <command>`.

- To see what an early phase makes of a program, stop after that phase: `parse` (a syntax check), `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` or `typecheck`.
- `unparse` prints the syntax tree back as Fortress source. Use it to see what a desugaring made.
- `link` links a compiled component (the `link` step of a compiled `.test` file). `api` writes a component's api. `test` runs a program's `test` declarations under walk.
- The command chooses the library. Walk and `test` call `Shell.useInterpreterLibraries()`. Every other command calls `useCompilerLibraries()`. Each call points `WellKnownNames` and `Types` to its prelude, and sets the desugaring switches.

## Where a test goes, and how it passes

Interpreter (walk): write `ProjectFortress/tests/Name.fss`, whose component is `Name`.

- Every `.fss` file there is gated, with no `.test` file needed.
- It is green if it throws no exception, exits 0, and neither its standard output nor its standard error contains `fail` or `FAIL`. A longer word counts too: `failure` fails the test. Only a file whose name contains `QuickCheckTest` is exempt.
- An api that it imports, and a helper component, go in `ProjectFortress/test_library/`. In `tests/`, a helper would run as a test.
- The harness skips files whose names end in `Syntax.fss`, `DynamicSemantics.fss` or `Satisfiability.fss`, or contain `GenomeUtil`.
- For a refusal at load, put `Name.test` beside `tests/Name.fss`, with `load_exception_contains=<message>`. A plain test is green if walk refuses the program at load as named. A failure while the top-level variables are initialised counts as a refusal. An `XXX` test here records a refusal that walk 

Compiled: write `Name.fss` and `Name.test` in the compiled test folder that holds tests of its kind:

- `library_tests/`: the compiler's library. A test of the interpreter's library is an interpreter test (above).
- `parser_tests/`: the parser.
### Compiled tests

Compiled tests are the `.test` files in `compiler_tests/`, `library_tests/` and `other_compiler_tests/`. They link with the library's jars in the tree's `default_repository/caches`. If a build started the caches again, or the tree's caches are empty, run the library order first (`build-and-caches.md`).

The script is `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh`. `climb-batch-N` is the folder's real name, not a placeholder. Run your own tree's copy: it runs the tree that it is in.

## One unit-test class, or one track

To run one unit-test class: `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=BitsJUTest`. It uses the tree's own caches and the shell's `FORTRESS_THREADS`.

To run tracks of testFast whole, run their target. Each target runs its tracks as testFast does, with the same JVMs and private caches:

- `ant testCompiler`: the compiler and othercompiler tracks.
- `ant testOtherCompiler`: the othercompiler track.
- `ant testLibrary`: the library track.
- `ant testQuick`: the three tracks.

- P-26 **The team's later decision wins over its earlier one, in a text or in code, where the team made it the language's rule.** P-7 names the texts, from the Working Draft to the POPL 2019 paper. Code counts as a decision where the team built it alike for all its types, or stated its rule in a commit message, a comment or the checker. Code that its author called a stub, and code that works around a limit of the JVM or of the checker, serve only the implementation. The decision that they depart from stands. "Later" is the date of the team's work on the point at issue. The revival revises `Specification/` to follow a later decision. The one library follows it too, in place of the team's earlier code, such as the interpreter's library. Where two later decisions conflict, the goal decides (P-8). The implementers' later word also outweighs unfinished text. Why: the Working Draft's early text was a wish. The type group, the part of the team that built the type checker and the compiler, then worked to make the language run. So they learned what is feasible. They sought performance, and specialization was a must. Their later decisions include the exclusion rule, specialization and the number types of the compiler's prelude, siblings from 2009 to 2012 (P-43). The revival knows less than they did, so it does not second-guess them.

content.content:
## What the compiled path cannot compile yet

For a construct that it cannot compile yet, the code generator calls `sayWhat` or throws another `CompilerError`. Such a call or throw is a code-generator wall. The code generator has no case for these constructs:

- `spawn`;
- an object expression;
- an array literal, such as `[1 2 3]`.

It compiles a local function as a closure, also one that calls itself or another local function of its block. It refuses these forms (ledger row 304):

- a local function with static parameters of its own: 'Can't compile a local function with static parameters of its own yet';
- two local functions of one name in a block: 'Can't compile overloaded local functions yet';
- a local function with the `atomic` modifier: 'Can't compile a local function with this modifier yet'.

A type assumption `e asif T` has the value of `e`, but the call around it chooses its declaration as if `e` were a `T`, a supertype of `e`'s type (`Specification/basic/expressions/type-annotation.tex`). The code generator compiles one at a dotted call's receiver, at a call of a functional method or an overloaded function whose e

- a call of a functional method or an overloaded function with an assumption at some of its arguments but not all: 'Can't compile a dispatched call whose arguments are not all type assumptions';
- a generic method on an assumed receiver: 'Can't compile a type assumption at the receiver of a generic method yet';
- a call of an overloaded generic function with an assumption at an argument: 'Can't compile a type assumption at a call of an overloaded generic function yet'.

It also refuses a function or method with a contract (`requires`, `ensures`, `invariant`). (* Members that a generic trait defines for a trait whose comprises clause lists it at a where-clause type variable compile and run: called functionally, dotted, and inside a generic function at its own type parameter (traits.tex, section "Trait Declarations": the listed type holds at every value of the variable). *)
component ComprisesWhereMemberCompiled
export Executable
trait AnyC comprises { C[\E\] } where [\E\]
  cat(self, f: AnyC): AnyC
  name(): String
  pair(a: String, b: String): String
end
trait C[\E\] extends AnyC
  cat(self, f: AnyC): AnyC = self
  name(): String = "C"
  pair(a: String, b: String): String = a || b
end
object Ci[\E\](item: E) extends C[\E\] end
which(x: AnyC): String =
  typecase x of
    Ci[\ZZ32\] => "first"
    else => "other"
  end
joined[\T\](c: C[\T\]): String = c.pair(c.name(), "d")
run(): () = do
  x: AnyC = cat(Ci[\ZZ32\](3), Ci[\String\]("s"))
  assert(which(x), "first", "the functional cat returns its first argument")
  assert(x.name(), "C", "the dotted name runs on a value of type AnyC")
  assert(joined[\ZZ32\](Ci[\ZZ32\](3)), "Cd", "the dotted pair runs inside a generic function")
  println("PASS")
end
end
(* A typecase in a generic function whose arms bind values at types that name the function's type parameters, and read them, compiles and runs each arm (typecase.tex, section "Typecase Expressions": the first clause that matches runs). *)
component TypecaseGenericArmsCompiled
export Executable
trait Shape end
object Sq extends Shape end
object Rd extends Shape end
trait Bx[\E\]
  size(): ZZ32
end
object B[\E\](k: ZZ32) extends Bx[\E\]
  size(): ZZ32 = k
end
sz[\X\](b: Bx[\X\]): ZZ32 = b.size()
app[\T, E extends T, F extends T\](a: Bx[\E\], b: Bx[\F\]): ZZ32 =
  typecase (a, b) of
    (a': Bx[\T\], b': Bx[\T\]) => sz[\T\](a') + sz[\T\](b')
    (a': Bx[\T\], b': Bx[\F\]) => 10 sz[\T\](a') + sz[\F\](b')
    (a': Bx[\E\], b': Bx[\T\]) => sz[\E\](a') + 10 sz[\T\](b')
    else => sz[\E\](a) - sz[\F\](b)
  end
run(): () = do
  assert(app[\Shape, Shape, Shape\](B[\Shape\](1), B[\Shape\](2)), 3, "both boxes of T")
  assert(app[\Shape, Shape, Sq\](B[\Shape\](1), B[\Sq\](2)), 12, "a box of T, then a box of F")
  assert(app[\Shape, Sq, Shape\](B[\Sq\](1), B[\Shape\](2)), 21, "a box of E, then a box of T")
  assert(app[\Shape, Sq, Rd\](B[\Sq\](1), B[\Rd\](2)), -1, "no arm, the else clause")
  println("PASS")
end
end
(* A conditional with self in one arm and a value of the self-type parameter in the other, returned at that parameter, runs compiled. *)
component SelfTypeArmRun
export Executable
trait Tord[\T extends Tord[\T\]\]
    lt(self, other: T): Boolean
    mx(self, other: T): T = if lt(other, self) then self else other end
end
object Num(v: ZZ32) extends Tord[\Num\]
    lt(self, other: Num): Boolean = v < other.v
end
run(): () = do
    assert(mx(Num(7), Num(5)).v, 7, "the arm that is self")
    assert(mx(Num(3), Num(5)).v, 5, "the arm that is the other value")
    println("PASS")
  end
end

(* A method or getter of either result type, called on a call typed by the intersection of its candidates' return types, or on a variable bound to it, gets the answer of the value's own object. *)
component CoverageReturnMethodCall
export Executable
trait S comprises { U, V } end
trait T comprises { V, W } end
trait U extends S excludes W end
trait M extends { S, T } comprises { V } end
trait V extends M end
trait W extends T end
object Vo extends V end
trait Tagged
  tag(): String = "tagged"
end
trait LeftResult extends Tagged
  getter side(): String = "left side"
  left(): String = "left"
  plusLeft(n: ZZ32): ZZ32 = n + 1
  get(n: ZZ32): String = "left at ZZ32"
  pick[\X extends Object\](x: X): X = x
end
trait RightResult extends Tagged
  right(): String = "right"
  get(s: String): String = "right at String"
end
object LeftOnly extends LeftResult end
object RightOnly extends RightResult end
object BothResult extends { LeftResult, RightResult }
  tag(): String = "both"
end
choose(s: S): LeftResult = LeftOnly
choose(t: T): RightResult = RightOnly
choose(v: V): BothResult = BothResult
run(): () = do
  m: M = Vo
  assert(choose(m).left(), "left", "a method of LeftResult on the call")
  assert(choose(m).right(), "right", "a method of RightResult on the call")
  assert(choose(m).side, "left side", "a getter of LeftResult on the call")
  assert(choose(m).plusLeft(41), 42, "a method with an argument on the call")
  assert(choose(m).tag(), "both", "a method that both result types inherit runs the object's own")
  assert(choose(m).get(5), "left at ZZ32", "an overloaded method's declaration in LeftResult")
  assert(choose(m).get("a"), "right at String", "an overloaded method's declaration in RightResult")
  assert(choose(m).pick[\String\]("picked"), "picked", "a generic method of LeftResult on the call")
  r = choose(m)
  assert(r.left(), "left", "a method of LeftResult on a variable bound to the call")
  assert(r.right(), "right", "a method of RightResult on a variable bound to the call")
  assert(r.side, "left side", "a getter of LeftResult on a variable bound to the call")
  println("PASS")
end
end

export Executable
object Mat(v: ZZ32)
    opr [i: ZZ32]: ZZ32 = v + i

    assert((mk())[5]^2, 36, "(mk())[5]^2")
    assert(Maker.f()[5]^2, 49, "Maker.f()[5]^2")

### A finding that would change a decision of the curator's

**Finding 1. Fork D1 and row 1064: the team's two untyped binder forms in a `typecase` arm. The default refused one and kept the other; the record showed him neither.**
- What is so:
  - The team's disambiguator read an arm that is a bare name naming no type as a binder over every value: `x =>` became `x: Any =>` (`TypeDisambiguator.java:246-250` at the base). It read a tuple of such names as a pattern of binders: `(x, y) =>` (`TypeDisambiguator.java:251-258`, `typeToPatternBinding`). The team's tests use one form each, `compiler_tests/Compiled7.PatternMatching.b.fss:30` (`x => println x`) and `Compiled7.PatternMatching.a.fss:30` (`(x, y) => println x`), both run by `AfterTypeChecking.test:16`.
  - Row 959's hazard is the bare form: since the merge, `Int =>` is a binder and takes every value.
  - Rung D refused the bare form, so `x =>` is now 'x is undefined.', and the team's test b was respelled `x: Any =>`. It kept the tuple form, so `(x, y) =>` binds, and `(Int, ZZ32) =>` takes every first element with no message (row 1064, CONTESTED; `tests/TypecaseTupleArmUndefinedNameBindsWalk.fss`). D.worker.1 and D.skeptic.1 put the tuple form to him.
  - The record's section for him showed `Int =>` only ("After: it is refused: 'Int is undefined.'"). It did not say that the team's bare binder ends.
  - The sources split. The chapter's grammar reads every arm as types, `TypecaseTypes ::= ( TypeList ) | Type` (`Specification/basic/expressions/typecase.tex:69-71`), and "it is a static error for a reference to a name to occur where it is not in scope" (`basic/declarations.tex:571-572`): both untyped forms are errors. The team's code and its checker accept both, and the chapter's note says "This section should be revised according to the changes in the pattern matching proposal" (`typecase.tex:15`). ### A finding that would change a decision of the curator's

**Finding 1. Fork D1 and row 1064: the team's two untyped binder forms in a `typecase` arm. The default refused one and kept the other; the record showed him neither.**
- What is so:
  - The team's disambiguator read an arm that is a bare name naming no type as a binder over every value: `x =>` became `x: Any =>` (`TypeDisambiguator.java:246-250` at the base). It read a tuple of such names as a pattern of binders: `(x, y) =>` (`TypeDisambiguator.java:251-258`, `typeToPatternBinding`). The team's tests use one form each, `compiler_tests/Compiled7.PatternMatching.b.fss:30` (`x => println x`) and `Compiled7.PatternMatching.a.fss:30` (`(x, y) => println x`), both run by `AfterTypeChecking.test:16`.
  - Row 959's hazard is the bare form: since the merge, `Int =>` is a binder and takes every value.
  - Rung D refused the bare form, so `x =>` is now 'x is undefined.', and the team's test b was respelled `x: Any =>`. It kept the tuple form, so `(x, y) =>` binds, and `(Int, ZZ32) =>` takes every first element with no message (row 1064, CONTESTED; `tests/TypecaseTupleArmUndefinedNameBindsWalk.fss`). D.worker.1 and D.skeptic.1 put the tuple form to him.
  - The record's section for him showed `Int =>` only ("After: it is refused: 'Int is undefined.'"). It did not say that the team's bare binder ends.
  - The sources split. The chapter's grammar reads every arm as types, `TypecaseTypes ::= ( TypeList ) | Type` (`Specification/basic/expressions/typecase.tex:69-71`), and "it is a static error for a reference to a name to occur where it is not in scope" (`basic/declarations.tex:571-572`): both untyped forms are errors. The team's code and its checker accept both, and the chapter's note says "This section should be revised according to the changes in the pattern matching proposal" (`typecase.tex:15`). The one library writes neither untyped form; it writes typed names inside a clause, `(a': List[\T\], b': List[\T\]) =>` (`Library/List.fss:94`), which rung V now compiles. The peer languages that bind an untyped name in a pattern, as Scala's `case x =>`, tell it from a constant by a rule of the name's form; Fortress has no such rule.
- What it changes: P-26, "The team's later decision wins over its earlier one, in a text or in code, where the team made it the language's rule ... Code counts as a decision where the team built it alike for all its types, or stated its rule in a commit message, a comment or the checker." The team's checker accepts both forms. The landed default refuses one of them on the specification's rule and keeps the other on the team's code: two readings of one question.
- Options:
  - **1a. As landed.** The bare binder is refused; a binder over every value is written `x: Any =>`. The tuple of names binds, row 1064 stays CONTESTED, and the hazard of row 959 stands inside a tuple. Costs nothing.
  - **1b. One rule, the specification's: refuse an undefined name in a tuple of names too.** `(x, y) =>` is written `(x: Any, y: Any) =>`, and the team's test a is respelled as test b was. The hazard goes everywhere in an arm, and row 1064 closes. A small rung in the disambiguator (`typecaseTupleNames`, `:61`, `:246-248`) with one team line respelled; rung D, the whole rung with its skeptic, wrote 0.71M.
  - **1c. One rule, the team's code: restore the bare binder.** `x =>` binds again, and both untyped forms stay. Row 959 reopens: an arm at `Int` takes every value, unless a rule of the revival's own refuses the five removed names, which no source of the team's states.
- How they weigh: 1a keeps what landed but holds two rules for one question. 1b follows the grammar, the scope rule and the library's way of writing a binder with its type, and ends two forms of the team's that no library line uses. 1c follows the team's code and its tests, and brings back a silent wrong answer for a program that names a removed type, or needs a special rule.
- Recommended: 1b. The library and the grammar point the same way, and a binder keeps its form with a type, `x: Any`. If he takes 1b, V.worker.1's question goes with it: the specification states the typed names inside a clause, which the library writes, in an Appendix I entry.

- A **fork** is a design question with more than one way. A **default** is the way that the record chose before the run.
- An **arm** is one clause of a `typecase`. A **binder** is a name that an arm gives to the value that it takes.
- An **intersection** is a type of two types at once. A value of it is a value of each.

199	## Part 1. Conformance
200	
201	No departure from a decision of the curator's landed. One finding would change a decision of his if he takes another way than the default that landed; it holds nothing.
202	
203	### A finding that would change a decision of the curator's
204	
205	**Finding 1. Fork D1 and row 1064: the team's two untyped binder forms in a `typecase` arm. The default refused one and kept the other; the record showed him neither.**
206	- What is so:
207	  - The team's disambiguator read an arm that is a bare name naming no type as a binder over every value: `x =>` became `x: Any =>` (`TypeDisambiguator.java:246-250` at the base). It read a tuple of such names as a pattern of binders: `(x, y) =>` (`TypeDisambiguator.java:249-256` on `main`, `typeToPatternBinding`, which the rung left as it was). The team's tests use one form each, `compiler_tests/Compiled7.PatternMatching.b.fss:30` (`x => println x`) and `Compiled7.PatternMatching.a.fss:30` (`(x, y) => println x`), both run by `AfterTypeChecking.test:16`.
208	  - Row 959's hazard is the bare form: since the merge, `Int =>` is a binder and takes every value.
209	  - Rung D refused the bare form, so `x =>` is now 'x is undefined.', and the team's test b was respelled `x: Any =>`. It kept the tuple form, so `(x, y) =>` binds, and `(Int, ZZ32) =>` takes every first element with no message (row 1064, CONTESTED; `tests/TypecaseTupleArmUndefinedNameBindsWalk.fss`). D.worker.1 and D.skeptic.1 put the tuple form to him.
210	  - The record's section for him showed `Int =>` only ("After: it is refused: 'Int is undefined.'"). It did not say that the team's bare binder ends.
211	  - The sources split. The chapter's grammar reads every arm as types, `TypecaseTypes ::= ( TypeList ) | Type` (`Specification/basic/expressions/typecase.tex:69-71`), and "it is a static error for a reference to a name to occur where it is not in scope" (`basic/declarations.tex:571-572`): both untyped forms are errors. The team's code and its checker accept both, and the chapter's note says "This section should be revised according to the changes in the pattern matching proposal" (`typecase.tex:15`). The one library writes neither untyped form; it writes typed names inside a clause, `(a': List[\T\], b': List[\T\]) =>` (`Library/List.fss:94`), which rung V now compiles. The peer languages that bind an untyped name in a pattern, as Scala's `case x =>`, tell it from a constant by a rule of the name's form; Fortress has no such rule.
212	- What it changes: P-26, "The team's later decision wins over its earlier one, in a text or in code, where the team made it the language's rule ... Code counts as a decision where the team built it alike for all its types, or stated its rule in a commit message, a comment or the checker." The team's checker accepts both forms. The landed default refuses one of them on the specification's rule and keeps the other on the team's code: two readings of one question.
213	- Options:
214	  - **1a. As landed.** The bare binder is refused; a binder over every value is written `x: Any =>`. The tuple of names binds, row 1064 stays CONTESTED, and the hazard of row 959 stands inside a tuple. Costs nothing.
215	  - **1b. One rule, the specification's: refuse an undefined name in a tuple of names too.** `(x, y) =>` is written `(x: Any, y: Any) =>`, and the team's test a is respelled as test b was. The hazard goes everywhere in an arm, and row 1064 closes. A small rung in the disambiguator (`typecaseTupleNames`, `:61`, `:246-248`) with one team line respelled; rung D, the whole rung with its skeptic, wrote 0.71M.
216	  - **1c. One rule, the team's code: restore the bare binder.** `x =>` binds again, and both untyped forms stay. Row 959 reopens: an arm at `Int` takes every value, unless a rule of the revival's own refuses the five removed names, which no source of the team's states.
217	- How they weigh: 1a keeps what landed but holds two rules for one question. 1b follows the grammar, the scope rule and the library's way of writing a binder with its type, and ends two forms of the team's that no library line uses. 1c follows the team's code and its tests, and brings back a silent wrong answer for a program that names a removed type, or needs a special rule.
218	- Recommended: 1b. The library and the grammar point the same way, and a binder keeps its form with a type, `x: Any`. If he takes 1b, V.worker.1's question goes with it: the specification states the typed names inside a clause, which the library writes, in an Appendix I entry.
219	
220	### Findings for the record, with no decision of his changed
221	
222	- **Rung Q's class-file read keeps no cache, and falls back to the old load for a class that the loader generates** (section 2, Q2). By reading; no test holds a generic object that lists a self-typed trait first. For the speed phase and for row 1052's notes.
223	- **Rung I's choice among incomparable conjuncts changes no answer by the exclusion rule** (section 2, V.worker.2). By reading; review-routed.1's test is owed.
224	- **Rung S's property has no user in the tree, and it breaks the run's pairing** (section 2, S1).
225	- **Rung C's worker took its P-148 pair at load 10.10** beside rung S's suites; the skeptic's pair settled it (section 1, C).
226	- **Six sentences of the plan or its check were not what landed:**
227	  - fork S1's "the compile, the run and the harness's run step follow it", false for the property;
228	  - fork Q1's "the declared type", built as the conditional's own type, with a cast where none is needed;
229	  - rung Q's members, which named `forLetFn`, not edited, and not `localFunctionClosure`, edited;
230	  - fork I1's "the most specific where several do", silent where none is;
231	  - row 822's cause, named the kind environment; it came through a tuple pattern's unbound names (row 1066);
232	  - the estimate's figures for the skeptics and the fixed roles, taken from a run on another tier (section 5).
233	- **Q's skeptic wrote that "the commit stage's microGPT quick checks run the compiled path"** (`compile-ladder/rung-self-arm-closure/SKEPTIC.md`, item 4). They run under walk (`gate/summary.txt`, '# microgpt-walk'). The sentence weighed the class-file read's unmeasured cost against a check that does not reach it.
234	- **The skeptics' fixes were right and small:** one defect of a change (I's owner of a call with no arrow), five tests added or corrected, and eleven records corrected; no fix was contested.
235	
236	### Corrections owed in the record
237	
238	- **POSITIONS:** P-33 (`POSITIONS.md:30`), "one build serving both by a second set of the run time's value classes (F-353)". The landed selector serves both libraries from one build with one set (F-353, F-381). Already on his list, with the old and the new words after run 2 (`CLIMB-BATCH-33.md`, section 6, "For the record-landing workflow"). No other entry is made false.
239	- **FACTS, false or short, and not reworded by the gather or the review:**
240	  - F-34 (`FACTS.md:38`): true of `c3b16ef2d1`'s code, as the gather says; it lacks the after (section 3) and names rows 812, 822 and 540 as the walls of their kinds, each closed now.
241	  - F-385 (`FACTS.md:281`): true; it lacks the cache and the generated class (section 2, Q2).
242	  - F-377 (`FACTS.md:276`): true; its open line "a worker chose it, and the curator has not decided it" now covers a conditional's arm too, item 571's home.
243	  - Every other entry that names a closed row was rewritten in the rungs' commits or in `f470e902b9` (`RECORD.md`, "FACTS entries"; the review's fixes): F-9, F-76, F-175, F-181, F-225, F-281, F-282, F-293, F-352, F-353, F-361, F-363, F-369, F-379, F-380, F-381, F-384, and 14 re-anchored.
244	- **PLAN:** Part 4.
245	- **The review queue:** item 572 (`review-queue.md:282`) is built by rung Q; items 519 (`:292`, row 959), 540 (`:260`, row 1029) and 587 (`:301`, row 1060) are answered by closed rows; item 584 (`:298`) says "with rows 540 and 818", and row 540 is closed.
246	- **The ledger:** rows 1062 to 1075 filed, 1066 closed, 559 rewritten; nothing further owed but the homes of Part 4.

448	## The steps due before run 2
449	
450	1. **The landing's own steps** (`references/batch.md`, "The landing"): the batch's to-dos swept from the shared task list (tasks 33 to 37 were there at 22:34), and each decision named in one line.
451	2. **The routing that no list holds yet** (Part 4): the lines for rows 1062, 1063, 1065, 1067, 1069, 1070, 1071, 1072, 1073, 1074 and 1075; one review-queue item for run 1's sixteen forks; item 572 built, items 519, 540 and 587 answered, item 584 reworded; rung C's reserved point as one line for him; PLAN's lines of Part 4.
452	3. **The record's corrections** (Part 1): F-34's after, F-385's two points, and P-33's words as the record gives them, with his sight of the old and the new.
453	4. **The measure on the landed tree:** `explorations/compile-ladder/plan-31/probes/planner/codegen-measure.sh <scratch-worktree> <out-dir>`, once, in a scratch worktree seeded from a build of `d3747846c1`; the patch applies. Expected 12 to 14. F-34 and `PLAN.md:67` take both figures.
454	5. **Run 2's sections read again** (Part 5): R's mission and overlaps with rung V's analyzer and rung I's caller; G's line on `forLetFn`; the moved lines of N, G and R; N's names table by the selector's name; run 2's estimate by process finding 1.
455	6. **The record-landing workflow for run 1** (`tools/record-landing/README.md`, with `batch: '33'`, `base: '1609258002b016489c96bd6e438389e89773b9eb'`, `landing: 'd3747846c1'`), with Part 3's list for the skill writer. Run 2 then launches after its skill step, as the manual's routing gives it (`climb-batch-workflow.md`, "After the landing: the coordinator's routing", step 5): its rungs W, G and R write tests in S's track, which the skill does not yet name. His go covers both runs and says nothing of the skill step.
456	7. **His word on finding 1,** fork D1 and row 1064, which holds nothing: it landed at its default, and either other way is a small rung.
457	8. **The script, between the runs:** process finding 3 (a tool fix after the base); finding 1 for run 2's estimate. Finding 5 is in `8109b61c63`.
458	
459	## For the curator
460	
461	Run 1 of climb batch 33 ran from 17:42 UTC to 22:36 UTC on 17 November. In your time that is 18:42 to 23:36. It is pushed. All six tasks landed. No line of the model program changed. You gave the go at about 17:13 UTC. Every decision took the planner's default, and this section is your review of them.
462	
463	The words that this section uses:
464	- **Walk** is the interpreter. The **compiled path** checks a program with the **checker** and then writes JVM bytecode with the **code generator**. The **class loader** makes and loads the classes when the compiled program runs.
465	- The **prelude** is the small library that the compiled path uses by default. The **one library** is the library of the interpreter.
466	- The **selector** is the setting `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`. With it, the compile command reads the one library.
467	- A **row** is one known defect in the ledger. An **expected-failure test** is a test that is known to fail and is marked so.
468	- The **gate** is the full check before a run lands.
469	- A **task** is one change of the run. The record names it a rung. A **worker** is an agent that does one task. A **skeptic** is a second agent that examines the work of the worker.
470	- A **fork** is a design question with more than one way. A **default** is the way that the record chose before the run.
471	- An **arm** is one clause of a `typecase`. A **binder** is a name that an arm gives to the value that it takes.
472	- An **intersection** is a type of two types at once. A value of it is a value of each.
473	- The **measure** counts the declarations of the one library that the code generator refuses.
474	
475	**What each task changed.** Each program is shortened from the tests that landed.
476	
477	- **S. The compile command can read the one library.** The commands and the build changed.
